The Indonesian Language Defines Time by Sunlight

September 15, 2026

In many languages, there is a clear word representing the time before noon (in English, am), and the time after noon (pm). This is similar in Japanese (午後) or Chinese (下午). However, in Indonesian, the closest word representing the time before noon is pagi, which translates to morning. The time after noon is closely represented by siang, which closely translates to afternoonit doesn't directly translates to afternoon. But both pagi and siang are colloquially used differently to am and pm. For example, 11 am is not considered pagi anymore. Some Indonesians don't consider 10 am as pagi. Likewise, 2 pm is considered siang, but 4 pm is not siang anymore, it's sore. The distinction feels unnatural, but from my experience, the distinction comes from the heat or the sunlight intensityLoosely defined by me, not a scientific unit of measurement..

Indonesia is entirely in the tropical region of the globeThe world's climate regions. This means that the sunlight hours are almost the same all year. This could be the reason why the words used to indicate time correlate to how hot it is outside (or how strong the sun is). Pagi means before the heat of the sun is at peak. Siang is when the sun is hottest, when you better find some shades. Sore is when the sun is still out, but it's past its hottest. Petang indicates the absence of sunlight, but it's not quite the darkest of night (similar to evening). Finally, malam is just night.
